subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on organic chemistry, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain organic chemistry for GCSE simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Alkanes and alkenes: combustion, cracking and the bromine test
Alcohols and the production of ethanol
Condensation polymers and problems of polymer disposal

questions.lo: Crude oil and fractional distillation
questions.q: Crude oil is a mixture of mainly which type of compound?
questions.explain: Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons, compounds containing only hydrogen and carbon.

questions.lo: Crude oil and fractional distillation
questions.q: In fractional distillation, molecules with the highest boiling points are collected where in the column?
options: At the bottom, where it is hottest
At the very top with the gases
At the top, where it is coolest
questions.explain: Larger molecules have higher boiling points and condense low down, where the column is hottest. Smaller molecules with low boiling points rise to the cooler top.

questions.lo: Crude oil and fractional distillation
questions.q: How do the properties of fractions change as the hydrocarbon molecules get larger?
options: They become more volatile and flow more easily
They become more viscous and less flammable
questions.explain: As molecules get larger, the fractions become more viscous (thicker), less volatile, less flammable and have higher boiling points.

questions.lo: Alkanes and alkenes: combustion, cracking and the bromine test
questions.q: What are the products of the complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
questions.explain: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon in plenty of oxygen produces carbon dioxide and water.

questions.lo: Alkanes and alkenes: combustion, cracking and the bromine test
questions.q: Why is cracking of large hydrocarbon molecules carried out?
options: To make more useful smaller molecules such as petrol and alkenes
To turn alkenes into alkanes only
questions.explain: Cracking breaks large, less useful hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones, such as petrol-sized alkanes and alkenes (like ethene) used to make polymers.

questions.lo: Alkanes and alkenes: combustion, cracking and the bromine test
questions.q: An unknown hydrocarbon decolourises bromine water. What does this indicate?
questions.explain: Alkenes decolourise bromine water (orange to colourless) because of their reactive C=C double bond. Alkanes do not react.

questions.lo: Alkanes and alkenes: combustion, cracking and the bromine test
questions.q: What is the general formula of the alkenes?
questions.explain: Alkenes have the general formula CnH2n and contain one carbon-carbon double bond.

questions.lo: Homologous series and general formulae
questions.q: Members of the same homologous series share which feature?
options: The same general formula and functional group
The same number of carbon atoms
questions.explain: A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same general formula and functional group, similar chemical properties, and consecutive members differing by CH2.

questions.lo: Homologous series and general formulae
questions.q: Which is the correct molecular formula for propane (three carbons, an alkane)?
questions.explain: Using CnH2n+2 with n=3 gives C3H8 for propane.

questions.lo: Alcohols and the production of ethanol
questions.q: What is the functional group of an alcohol?
questions.explain: Alcohols contain the -OH (hydroxyl) functional group.

questions.lo: Alcohols and the production of ethanol
questions.q: In the fermentation of sugar to make ethanol, which conditions are needed?
options: High temperature and a nickel catalyst
Yeast, warm conditions (about 30 C) and no air
questions.explain: Fermentation uses yeast in warm conditions (around 30 C) in the absence of air. Enzymes in the yeast convert sugar (glucose) into ethanol and carbon dioxide.

questions.lo: Alcohols and the production of ethanol
questions.q: Ethanol can also be manufactured by reacting ethene with steam. This method is a form of:
questions.explain: Ethene reacts with steam (using a phosphoric acid catalyst) in a hydration/addition reaction to produce ethanol.

questions.lo: Carboxylic acids and esters
questions.q: Which functional group is present in a carboxylic acid such as ethanoic acid?
questions.explain: Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group, -COOH.

questions.lo: Carboxylic acids and esters
questions.q: An ester is made by reacting a carboxylic acid with which compound (using an acid catalyst)?
questions.explain: Esters are formed when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol, usually in the presence of a concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst.

questions.lo: Carboxylic acids and esters
questions.q: What is commonly noticed about many esters?
options: They are all gases at room temperature
They often have sweet, fruity smells
questions.explain: Esters often have pleasant, sweet, fruity smells and are used in flavourings and perfumes.

questions.lo: Addition polymerisation
questions.q: Poly(ethene) is formed from ethene monomers by which process?
questions.explain: Poly(ethene) is formed by addition polymerisation: many ethene monomers with C=C bonds join together to form a long chain with no other product.

questions.lo: Addition polymerisation
questions.q: Which feature must a monomer have to undergo addition polymerisation?
questions.explain: Addition polymerisation requires monomers with a carbon-carbon double bond (C=C), which opens up to join with other monomers.

questions.lo: Condensation polymers and problems of polymer disposal
questions.q: How does condensation polymerisation differ from addition polymerisation?
options: A small molecule such as water is lost when the monomers join
It uses monomers with C=C bonds only
questions.explain: In condensation polymerisation, monomers (each with two functional groups) join together and a small molecule such as water is lost each time. Nylon and polyester are made this way.

questions.lo: Condensation polymers and problems of polymer disposal
questions.q: Why do many polymers cause environmental problems when thrown away?
options: They are non-biodegradable and are not broken down by microbes
questions.explain: Many polymers are non-biodegradable, so microbes cannot break them down. They persist in landfill and the environment for a very long time.

questions.lo: Condensation polymers and problems of polymer disposal
questions.q: Which is a drawback of disposing of polymers by burning (incineration)?
options: It can release toxic gases and carbon dioxide
It has no effect on the environment
questions.explain: Burning polymers can release toxic gases (such as hydrogen chloride from PVC) and carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, so incineration must be carefully controlled.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Chemistry (4CH1) specification; Organic Chemistry
